sweep_summary: Momu-Fas (fass1245) is in the catalog as not determinable on Honeyman 2017 p.461 (compound bears a single prominent accent; no placement rule). this search of works with stress in the title's only keyword item, Brendel & Ackermann 2009 'Foreign Accent Syndrome (FAS)', is a neurology chapter matched on the language name and is irrelevant (Crossref record confirms; paywalled; priority none). Re-read the three SIL Fas phonology documents already held by the project from the 9/16 check and the Honeyman thesis text: Baron 2007 (p.6) and Baron 1983c (pp.3, 6) attest stress as a conditioning factor ('unstressed syllables and heavily stressed syllables'; '/ey/ and /ow/ only occur in stressed open syllables'; 'a fuller analysis of stress' still needed), and the SIL OPD's Suprasegmentals section is blank; the OPD's acute accents mark mid vowels, not stress. Honeyman's compound passage re-read verbatim, matches the catalog quote; his phonology chapter has no stress section. No source states where word stress falls, so the classification stays not determinable with Baron 2007 as supporting evidence that word stress exists. Glottolog's only other sketch, Blake 2007 'Spatial Reference in Momu' (Sydney thesis), has no open copy located (low priority).

new_statements.quote: [ə] in Fas occurs in closed syllables, unstressed syllables and heavily stressed syllables. It may be inserted between incompatible consonant sequences. It has not been noticed to occur word finally. There is some evidence that it represents /i/ in these positions.
new_statements.citation: Baron, Wietze. 2007. Overview of Fas Phonology. Ms, 8 pp. SIL PNG (SIL Language & Culture Archives item 50902).
new_statements.reading: The SIL fieldworker who worked on Fas for decades treats stress as a real, gradient property of Fas syllables (unstressed vs heavily stressed) that conditions schwa, and in his 1983 orthography paper also ties /ey/ /ow/ to 'stressed open syllables' while conceding stress has not been fully analysed. This is independent first-hand confirmation that Momu-Fas has word-level stress, but neither Baron paper nor Honeyman 2017 states where it falls, so the catalog's not determinable (accent exists per phonological word, position unstated) stands.

new_statements.quote: Momu has at least five vowel phonemes, with the possible addition of schwa or a similar centralised vowel. It appears that schwa only occurs in unstressed and closed syllables, for example əsəmwa 'mosquito' and fək 'house', however this hypothesis needs to be confirmed by further investigation.

new_statements.relation_note: Independently repeats Baron's observation (Baron 2007 SHWA section; Baron 1983 note 3) that schwa is tied to unstressed syllables, i.e. presupposes that Momu has word stress, but like Baron gives no placement. Consistent with the catalog's 'accent exists, position undetermined' entry and with the existing Baron 2007 statement; adds nothing on placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule given. The grammar sketch (sec. 1.4.1) covers only the consonant and vowel inventories and the orthography; stress appears once, presupposed as a property of syllables (schwa restricted to 'unstressed and closed syllables', flagged as an unconfirmed hypothesis). Nothing on where word stress falls, on contrastiveness, or on tone. Full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/tone/pitch/prosody returned this single substantive hit.
new_statements.identity_note: Blake 2007 describes the Momu spoken at Mori village (sec. 1.2.2), West Sepik, from 2006-07 fieldwork; Baron 1983 describes Fas of the Kilifas area (West Sepik / Sandaun), 1978-88 fieldwork. Both are the same language (Momu = Fas, fass1245); no dialect-level difference in the stress remarks.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author and same substance as the existing Baron 2007 statement (schwa conditioned by stress; /ey/ /ow/ in stressed open syllables). Confirms that Momu-Fas has word-level stress with phonological effects but gives no placement, so it supports the catalog's 'accent exists, position not determinable' entry and does not refine it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule. The paper is about orthography design (phonemic vs transition principle) and mentions stress only as a conditioning factor: schwa arises from /e/ in closed or unstressed syllables and might be non-phonemic once stress is analysed; the complex nuclei /ey/ and /ow/ (the 'high vowels' I and U) occur only in stressed open syllables. Stress is treated as real and word-internal but explicitly 'not fully analysed'; where it falls is never stated. The acute accents in the orthography (é, ó) mark vowel quality (note 4), not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Blake 2007 describes the Momu spoken at Mori village (sec. 1.2.2), West Sepik, from 2006-07 fieldwork; Baron 1983 describes Fas of the Kilifas area (West Sepik / Sandaun), 1978-88 fieldwork. Both are the same language (Momu = Fas, fass1245); no dialect-level difference in the stress remarks.
